section: Knowledge Gaps and the New Tools
text: The project lacked a tested way to connect its neural controllers to the human reference and artificial-muscle models and evaluate them under comparable conditions. The missing capability was more specific than generating rhythmic joint motion. I needed to choose a controller, define the mechanical model and sensory inputs, specify how the body was supported, and measure what changed after a controlled intervention. Without those controls, an improvement in motion could not be assigned to neural feedback, muscle mechanics, or external support.

concern: Ben reply: per-leg PF organization and MN feedback
text: For a course project in ME 610: Neuromechanical Modeling, Morrow and I combined the bipedal mechanics of \citet{li_bipedal_2017} with the two-level central pattern generator (CPG) of \citet{deng_neuromechanical_2019} in AnimatLab \citep{cofer_animatlab_2010}. The mechanical model had a pelvis and bilateral thigh, shank, foot, and toe segments, with sagittal-plane joints and antagonist Hill-type muscles at the hip, knee, and ankle. I added a passive toe joint. The initial controller used one rhythm generator (RG) to control both sides, with separate pattern-formation (PF) groups for each leg: one for the hip and one for the knee and ankle. The shared RG layer contained four neurons. We added afferent feedback at the motoneuron (MN) level. Figure~\ref{fig:animatlab_model_architecture}(A) shows the mechanical model, and Figure~\ref{fig:animatlab_model_architecture}(B) shows the original shared-RG controller that Morrow and I built.

concern: Actual conversion failures and robot-first attempt
text: My first conversion attempt used the robot model, which combined BPA routing on the Gait2392 skeleton with unchanged human muscle parameters. MyoConverter's muscle-equilibrium checks rejected infeasible combinations of routed length and muscle parameters. I therefore separated conversion of the human reference from reconstruction of the robot routing. This distinction matters because an error caused by an artificial-actuator route should not be interpreted as a property of the original human model.

text: A separate Simulink implementation of a Deng-derived RG/PF circuit, with a fixed sodium-inactivation time constant of \qty{350}{\milli\second}, produced ten bursts over \qty{20}{\second} following a single \qty{10}{\nano\ampere}, \qty{1}{\milli\second} pulse. Its period was \qty{1.938}{\second}, compared with approximately \qty{1.94}{\second} in our NumPy reference, which was itself translated from the Nourse/Deng parameter tables. This test demonstrates self-sustained activity after a brief input, unlike the contact-driven comparison above. The original Deng AnimatLab project was extracted for connectivity and parameters but was not run for this comparison. The published Deng perturbation experiment therefore remains untested in translation. This comparison also does not demonstrate pointwise voltage agreement: the logged maximum voltage differences were approximately \qty{63}{\milli\volt}.

text: The Simulink air-stepping demonstration connects eight BPA-force elements to two planar legs with a fixed pelvis and no ground contact. It establishes that neural commands can drive the actuator and joint calculations together. However, the approximately \qty{0.31}{\second} swing period differed substantially from the RG period of \qty{1.938}{\second}. The observed limb oscillation therefore does not establish that the mechanics follow the neural rhythm. Mechanical imports from OpenSim and SolidWorks remain another stage of integration; the standalone reflex and air-stepping demonstrations do not establish control of those imported mechanisms.

concern: W2L mass changes, support, and robustness
text: The corrected candidate was also tested with thigh or distal-leg masses and inertias changed by $\pm10$ and $\pm20$ percent, and whole-leg properties changed by $\pm10$ percent. All ten conditions retained bilateral contact cycling, but nine exceeded the \ang{45} tilt gate. Only one condition passed the recorded survival criterion. Minimum pelvis height across these records was approximately \qty{0.898}{\metre}. This is evidence of persistent cycling with inadequate posture robustness, rather than ten successful robust-walking tests.

text: The W2L tests examine whether a controller retains bilateral contact cycling when the body or selected neural pathways change. An implementation check showed that the initial search applied only six of the 61 saved parameter fields; the other 55 fields did not reach the model. Those records describe a controller with the remaining pathways at their default strengths. The results reported here use a later replay with the stored individual fields applied. Because those values had not been optimized under the corrected mapping, this replay tests a candidate controller rather than a newly optimized solution.

text: With the stored individual fields applied and settings held fixed, the control completed 17 left and 16 right heel-contact cycles during the \qty{16}{\second} record (Figure~\ref{fig:w2l_perturbation}). Removing the crossed heel pathway produced 16/16 cycles, the Ia chain 13/13, the Renshaw pathways 16/14, the heel cascade 17/15, and commissural coupling 13/12. Removing Ib load feedback produced no heel-contact cycles on either side. The specific result is that Ib feedback was necessary for contact cycling in this configuration, while commissural removal reduced the count without abolishing it. Contact counts alone do not show that phase, posture, or gait quality remained unchanged.

text: A separate controller derived from \citet{dirusso_investigating_2023} was coupled to the Gait2392 human model. It uses per-muscle reflex parameters and a staged optimization procedure, with changes to the source model and optimization method. The recorded second-stage stability search completed 120 trials without a configuration passing its survival criterion. This is a negative result for that implementation and search, rather than a reproduction of the published walking result. It also shows why completing a connectome transcription or obtaining a fitted neural output cannot substitute for testing the coupled mechanics.

text: The present contribution is a usable framework for developing and testing neuromechanical controllers, with demonstrated components and explicit limits. Establishing a general biological mechanism will require matched interventions and comparisons with the corresponding biological or published-model results. Achieving unsupported walking will require further balance and weight-bearing control. The framework makes those questions accessible to controlled simulation; it does not resolve them by the existence of a tuned trajectory. Chapter~\ref{ch:futurework} discusses the remaining integration and hardware work.

concern: Selected Rybak published neural behaviors reproduced with documented reductions
text: An activity-based reduction of the two-level circuit of \citet{rybak_modelling_2006} was tested against selected published neural behaviors. At the published drive settings, increasing extensor drive produced a longer extensor phase, while increasing flexor drive reversed that relationship. The deletion tests distinguished the two circuit levels: a PF-level pulse suppressed flexor MN bursts without resetting the RG schedule, whereas an RG-level pulse shifted the subsequent rhythm. The first returning flexor burst differed from the extrapolated schedule by 0.001 periods after the PF perturbation and 0.416 periods after the RG perturbation. All 13 specified checks passed, including deterministic repeat runs.
change: Selected Rybak published neural behaviors reproduced with documented reductions

concern: Human wean removes added hand drive, not all descending drive or all feedback
text: The human-model feedback-tuning campaign provides a complementary test of sustained activity. With the selected feedback parameters fixed, bilateral stepping-like motion persisted as the added hand-drive currents were reduced to zero, with 8 and 11 contact cycles at zero scale. The original feedback configuration lost bilateral activity below 0.85 of those added currents. However, the descending drive remained active, the mechanics retained support, and the motion was in place. This comparison tests the effect of feedback re-tuning on dependence on added drive; it is not a fixed-controller feedback-intact versus feedback-disabled experiment. A matched feedback-ablation pair on the walking BPA model remains absent.
change: Human wean removes added hand drive, not all descending drive or all feedback
